report: Skin biopsy showing a monomorphic perivascular/adnexal atypical T-cell infiltrate with aberrant CD4/CD8 coexpression and abnormal flow cytometry, together with splenomegaly and lymphadenopathy, strongly supports T-cell lymphoma with secondary vasculitic ulceration. Doppler ultrasound indicating venous stasis as secondary and pathological exclusion of Behçet disease/primary vasculitis/thrombotic APS refute alternative hypotheses. However, TCR gene rearrangement and bone marrow studies are unavailable, so T-cell clonality is not definitively confirmed; the diagnosis is favored but not proven. No further subtyping is possible from current evidence.

Post-traumatic angioinvasive fungal infection explains the right lower leg swelling. Evidence: plant trauma, immunosuppression, necrotic ulcers, biopsy with septate hyphae and vascular occlusion, PAS-positive non-melanized hyphae, culture-confirmed fungus with appressoria. This refutes malignancy and inflammatory ulcer; infected venous stasis ulcer is less likely. Missing bacterial culture and MRI/CT leave secondary bacterial infection and deep extension possible but unconfirmed.

The patient's presentation is best explained by severe viral pneumonia due to COVID-19. Positive SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR directly confirms infection, and CTPA showing multifocal ground-glass opacities without pulmonary embolism is characteristic of viral pneumonia. Unvaccinated older age, progression to ARDS requiring intubation and proning, and acute kidney failure all support severe COVID-19. Bacterial pneumonia with sepsis and non-infectious ARDS are unlikely because the viral etiology is confirmed and no bacterial pathogen or non-infectious cause has been identified. The evidence strongly converges on severe COVID-19 pneumonia as the cause of the patient's respiratory failure.

The patient's verrucoid keratotic papules after laser resurfacing, on a background of photodamage and prior basal cell carcinoma, failed conservative therapy. Two biopsies showed verrucous actinic keratosis with atypical squamous proliferation and no koilocytes or viral cytopathic effect, strongly supporting a precancerous keratosis and excluding viral wart and benign keratotic papules. Lack of response to topical treatment argues against dermatitis. Although HPV PCR/genotyping was not performed, leaving minor uncertainty, the evidence strongly favors verrucous actinic keratosis, a specific precancerous lesion, refining the broader frontier of skin cancer or precancer.

The patient's chronic noninfectious bilateral uveitis, recurrent cystoid macular edema, and dexamethasone implant treatment strongly support an inflammatory mechanism. Imaging showing the implant adherent to the retina with indentation/compression and linear hyperautofluorescence in the superior macula further corroborates inflammation. Post-surgical ERM is less supported despite pseudophakia, injections, and gas tamponade. Vitreoretinal disease has minimal support, and idiopathic ERM is refuted by the inflammatory context and imaging findings. Therefore, the epiretinal membrane is best explained as inflammatory.

Histopathology shows filarial parasite cross-sections with microfilariae in a gravid uterus, confirming a parasitic filarial nodule and supporting the infectious/inflammatory hypothesis while ruling out tumor/cyst and malignancy. Negative blood smear plus tissue microfilariae indicates occult filarial infection, the most refined frontier. Unavailable serology/ultrasound only limits species identification, not the diagnosis.

Histology showed graft detachment caused by a donor-derived epithelial cyst containing cellular debris, positive cytokeratin and male donor origin; AS-OCT hyperdensity matched a cellular cyst. No microbiological proof of infection was present. These findings support donor-derived epithelial cyst (score 0.9) and progressive enlargement explains delayed worsening. Infection, rejection, and recurrence were refuted by histology and expert interpretation. Therefore, the cause is a donor epithelial cyst.

Immunocompromised patient with fever, dyspnea, cough; CT showing only bronchiectasis excludes opportunistic pneumonia. CMV viral load rising from 63 to 3171 IU/mL despite antiviral therapy, glans ulceration, and severe immunosuppression converge on disseminated CMV infection. UL97/UL54 resistance mutations may explain the rise. HSV, mycobacterial, fungal, heart failure, and bronchiectasis exacerbation are less supported. Pending histopathology/CMV PCR prevents absolute certainty.

The postpartum woman presents with right breast erythema, pain, recurrent episodes, and bilateral milky discharge. Laboratory tests show leukocytosis and elevated CRP, and milk culture grew penicillin-susceptible Streptococcus agalactiae, confirming a bacterial infectious etiology. Ultrasound reveals no abscess or focal lesion, and physical exam shows no fluctuance, effectively excluding breast abscess and inflammatory breast cancer. Milk stasis remains a secondary contributor but is not the primary process. The evidence converges on high-confidence lactational mastitis caused by S. agalactiae, with confidence 0.9, and no further refinement is needed for clinical diagnosis.

The patient's hoarseness, dysphagia, vomiting, headache, and right CN IX–XII palsy localize to the skull base/jugular foramen. MRI shows a jugular foramen tumor with smooth rim enhancement and extrinsic compression; pathology confirms PEComa with HMB-45, Melan-A, and TFE3 positivity and S-100 negativity. These are definitive neoplastic findings. Normal coagulation, extrinsic compression rather than intrinsic thrombosis, and absent tuberous sclerosis history refute vascular/thrombotic, inflammatory/infectious, and genetic syndrome lesions. Thus the diagnosis is PEComa of the jugular foramen/skull base.
